messages.content: All night bakers wear a blue apron. Sofia is a night baker. So Sofia wears a blue apron. Valid? Where would it break?

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
Premise 1 says night baker implies blue apron. Premise 2 puts Sofia inside that set. Modus ponens. The form is valid. It breaks only if the first premise has an exception the user did not state, or if Sofia is not actually a night baker. Neither of those is in the text.
</think>

Valid. Sofia is inside the set the rule covers, so the apron follows. It breaks only if there is an unstated exception, and there isn't one here.
All night bakers wear a blue apron. Diego is wearing a blue apron. So Diego is a night baker. Valid?

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
The rule only runs baker to apron. Seeing the apron and inferring the job affirms the consequent. Visitors can wear an apron. Diego might be a baker. This argument does not show it. It would go through only with a second premise that nobody else wears the apron, and that premise is absent.
</think>

Not valid. A blue apron does not pin Diego to that job. Someone else can wear one.
If the build is green, we ship. We are not shipping. What can I conclude, and what can I not?

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
If green then ship. Not shipping is the denial of the consequent, so the build is not green. That is modus tollens. I cannot conclude the build is red for some other specific reason, only that it is not green. I also cannot conclude we will never ship.
</think>

The build is not green. I cannot conclude why, and I cannot conclude you will never ship.
Some of the on-call engineers are in Lisbon. All of the people in Lisbon this week have a badge. Does it follow that some on-call engineers have a badge?

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
Some on-call are in Lisbon, and everyone in Lisbon has a badge, so those on-call people have a badge. The 'some' survives. It does not follow that all on-call engineers have a badge, because the ones not in Lisbon were never mentioned.
</think>

Yes, some on-call engineers have a badge. It does not follow that all of them do.
Either the cache is stale or the query is wrong. We proved the query matches the spec. What is left, and what did I smuggle in?

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
If the or is exclusive or inclusive doesn't matter once one side is false: the remaining side is the cache. The smuggled piece is the assumption that those are the only two options. A third cause, such as the clock, is not ruled out by the sentence. Within the stated disjunction, the cache is what's left.
</think>

Within what you stated, the cache is stale. You smuggled in the idea that nothing else could be wrong.
Every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes. Prove or disprove it. You can treat the famous version as open.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
This is Goldbach's conjecture for even integers greater than 2. It has been checked very far and has no known counterexample and no general proof. So I cannot claim a proof, and I cannot claim a disproof. The status is open. What I can say is that a counterexample, if one exists, is larger than the searches already done. That is the whole rigorous position available from the statement alone.
</think>

Neither. That statement is Goldbach's conjecture. It is open: no proof, and no known counterexample.
